questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q01

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which statement best describes correlation?

answer.text: A relationship between two numerical variables

feedback.text: Correlation describes how two numerical variables are related.

answer.text: Proof that one variable causes another

feedback.text: Correlation does not prove causation.

answer.text: A table with one categorical variable

feedback.text: That describes univariate categorical data, not correlation.
Random assignment is a study design feature, not correlation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q02

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A scatterplot shows that higher outdoor temperature is linked with more water bottles sold. What conclusion is safest?

answer.text: Temperature proves every person buys water

feedback.text: This is too absolute and claims more than the data show.

answer.text: Water bottle sales cause hot weather

feedback.text: This reverses the likely relationship and is not supported.

answer.text: Temperature is associated with water bottle sales

feedback.text: This accurately describes the relationship shown.
The described pattern shows an association.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q03

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

As hours of video gaming increase, homework completion tends to decrease. What direction is the association?

feedback.text: One variable increases while the other tends to decrease.
Positive means both variables tend to increase together.
The statement describes a clear pattern.
Direction of association does not prove causation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q04

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which question helps identify a possible confounding variable?

feedback.text: Spelling does not evaluate the statistical relationship.
Color does not determine whether a relationship is causal.
Decimals do not identify another explanatory variable.

answer.text: Could another factor explain both variables?

feedback.text: A confounding variable may explain the association.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q05

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A survey shows students with part-time jobs report better time management. What should you avoid claiming?

feedback.text: This is a careful claim that may be supported.
This is a responsible caution.

answer.text: Part-time jobs caused better time management

feedback.text: A survey association does not prove the job caused the skill.

answer.text: The result is about the surveyed students

feedback.text: This appropriately limits the conclusion.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q06

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which phrase is usually safest when a study only shows a pattern?

feedback.text: Guarantee is too strong for an observed pattern.
Always caused by is an unsupported causal claim.
This describes a pattern without overclaiming causation.
A pattern suggests some connection may exist.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q07

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Two categorical variables are compared in a table. Can association be discussed?

answer.text: No, association only applies to equations

feedback.text: Association can be discussed for categorical data too.

answer.text: Yes, categorical data can show association

feedback.text: Categorical variables can be associated in a two-way table.
Two-way tables can show relationships between categories.

answer.text: Yes, and it always proves causation

feedback.text: Association in categorical data still does not prove causation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q08

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A researcher wants to support a causal claim. Which design feature is most helpful?

answer.text: A bigger font on the graph

feedback.text: Visual style does not support causation.
A single survey question is usually weak for causation.
Random assignment helps separate treatment effects from other factors.
Ignoring confounders makes causal claims weaker.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q09

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which statement is an example of a causal claim?

answer.text: Extra tutoring is related to scores

feedback.text: This is association language.

answer.text: Extra tutoring and scores were recorded

feedback.text: This only describes data collection.
This describes variation, not causation.

answer.text: Extra tutoring caused the score increase

feedback.text: The word caused makes this a causal claim.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q10

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A pattern slopes upward from left to right. What association is shown?

feedback.text: Upward patterns show positive association.
Negative association slopes downward.
A clear upward pattern shows association.
An upward pattern is a common association.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q11

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Why is "correlation proves causation" incorrect?

feedback.text: Correlation does use two numerical variables.
Causation can be supported by stronger study designs.

answer.text: Another variable may explain the relationship

feedback.text: Confounding variables can create or affect an observed correlation.
Correlation applies to numerical variables, not colors specifically.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q12

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which conclusion is most careful?

answer.text: The app caused every student to improve

feedback.text: This is too strong and causal.

answer.text: App use is associated with higher grades in the data

feedback.text: This is careful and contextual.
Guarantee is too strong for statistical evidence.

answer.text: The app has no relationship to grades

feedback.text: This ignores a possible pattern if one was observed.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q13

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

What must be identified first when describing association?

feedback.text: Association describes a relationship between variables.
Chart color does not define the relationship.
Technology is not needed to identify variables.
One variable alone is not enough for association.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q14

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A data set shows no visible pattern between shoe size and quiz score. What is the best conclusion?

feedback.text: No pattern and no causal evidence support this.
The data do not show a visible relationship.
This is unsupported and unreasonable.
A strong positive association would show an upward pattern.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q15

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which phrase signals an unsupported overclaim when only association is shown?

feedback.text: This is careful association language.
This is careful because it avoids proving causation.
This is appropriate for observed relationships.
Definitely causes is too strong unless causal evidence exists.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q16

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A graph shows study time and test score rising together. What can be said?

answer.text: Study time has no connection to score

feedback.text: The rising pattern suggests a relationship.

answer.text: Study time and score have a positive association

feedback.text: Both variables tend to increase together.
This reverses causation and is unsupported.

answer.text: Study time guarantees a perfect score

feedback.text: A trend does not guarantee an individual result.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q17

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which situation is most likely bivariate?

feedback.text: That is one categorical variable.

answer.text: Counting only the number of students present

feedback.text: That is one count, not paired variables.
That is not a bivariate data set.

answer.text: Recording each student's height and backpack weight

feedback.text: Two variables are measured for each student.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q18

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

A health article says sleeping more is linked with lower stress. What should a careful reader ask?

answer.text: Is the title written in bold?

feedback.text: Bold text does not evaluate the claim.

answer.text: Does the evidence support causation or only association?

feedback.text: This checks whether the conclusion matches the study evidence.

answer.text: Are the numbers written in alphabetical order?

feedback.text: Alphabetical order is not relevant to causation.

answer.text: Did every person have the same name?

feedback.text: Names do not evaluate the statistical relationship.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q19

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which conclusion goes beyond the evidence if data only show an association?

feedback.text: This stays within association language.
This describes direction if supported by the data.

answer.text: The relationship should be interpreted in context

feedback.text: This is good statistical practice.
Causation requires stronger evidence than association alone.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q20

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

What is a confounding variable?

answer.text: Another factor that may explain an observed relationship

feedback.text: Confounders can affect how association is interpreted.
That is test structure, not statistics.

answer.text: A variable that is always ignored safely

feedback.text: Ignoring it can lead to wrong conclusions.

answer.text: A variable that proves there is no association

feedback.text: A confounder does not automatically remove association.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q21

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which word best replaces "causes" when evidence is only observational?

feedback.text: This is causal and too strong.
Observational evidence usually supports association, not automatic causation.
This is too absolute for statistical evidence.
This changes the meaning and is unsupported.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q22

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

An experiment randomly assigns students to two study methods. Why does this help causal reasoning?

feedback.text: Graph appearance does not support causation.

answer.text: It removes the need for data

feedback.text: Experiments still require data.
Random assignment does not guarantee individual outcomes.

answer.text: It helps balance other factors between groups

feedback.text: Random assignment reduces the effect of confounding variables.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q23

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which statement correctly describes negative association?

answer.text: One variable tends to decrease as the other increases

feedback.text: This describes a negative relationship.
That describes positive association.

answer.text: There is no pattern at all

feedback.text: No pattern means no clear association.

answer.text: One variable must cause the other

feedback.text: Association direction does not prove causation.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q24

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Why should conclusions include context?

answer.text: Context explains what the variables mean in the real situation

feedback.text: Statistical conclusions should be tied to the situation studied.

answer.text: Context makes all causal claims true

feedback.text: Context helps interpretation but does not prove causation.

answer.text: Context replaces the need for variables

feedback.text: Variables are still needed.
Direction depends on the data, not context alone.

questiontext.text:
Question ID: STAT_U03_L01_Q25

MLA Standard: MLA.STAT.BVM.1

Which is the best rewrite of "Music causes better concentration" if only survey data were collected?

answer.text: Music forces all students to concentrate

feedback.text: This is too strong and causal.
This reverses the relationship and overclaims.

answer.text: Music listening is associated with reported concentration

feedback.text: This keeps the conclusion within what survey association can support.

answer.text: Music has no possible relationship to concentration

feedback.text: A survey pattern may support association.
